extracted.intended_audience: students, scholars, and policymakers studying federal constitutions and comparative government
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and standards for judging the design, strengths, weaknesses, and suitability of federal (confederate vs. national) constitutions, drawn from a political-theory chapter describing the American federal system. Useful for constitutional designers, comparative analysts, and students of political institutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid concentration of legislative power
rubrics_metrics.description: To concentrate the whole social force in the hands of the legislative body is the natural tendency of democracies; this concentration is prejudicial to a well-conducted administration and favorable to the despotism of the majority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legislatures that monopolize influence can subordinate executive and judicial functions; designers should prevent legislative predominance (the founders of the Union resisted these democratic propensities). Examples/anti-patterns: State legislatures that control executive salary and committees, producing a passive executive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Executive independence and strength
rubrics_metrics.description: The Federal Constitution vests all the privileges and all the responsibility of the executive power in a single individual and strives to confer a strong and independent position upon the executive authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Features cited as securing independence: fixed presidential duration (four years), salary not alterable during term, official dependents, suspensive veto. Contrast with State executives who are temporaries or subject to legislative control (e.g., salary removal, committees usurping execution).

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial independence
rubrics_metrics.description: The Federal Constitution carefully separates the judicial authority from all external influences and provides for the independence of the judges.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guarantees include immutable tenure and salaries that shall not be altered; contrasted with States where legislatures regulate judges' emoluments or temporarily appoint judges, subjecting them to influence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Federal government must execute its own laws (self-derived force)
rubrics_metrics.description: Unlike earlier confederations in which the Federal Government dictated laws but left execution to member States, the American Constitution provides that the Federal Government should not only dictate laws but execute its own enactments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical consequence: a federal authority that can implement policies via its own civil and military officers, courts, and army rather than relying on requisitions from member states.

rubrics_metrics.name: Federal government must be able to levy and collect taxes directly on individuals
rubrics_metrics.description: In America the national Government levies a tax not upon the State but upon each inhabitant; it rules individuals and has self-derived force.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This direct taxation reduces the ability of member states to evade federal demands (contrast with prior confederations where federal demands were supplied by states and easily resisted). Ensures enforceability of federal policy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Means of enforcement should match nominal powers
rubrics_metrics.description: The real weakness of federal governments has almost always been in the exact ratio of their nominal power; federal strength depends on having the means to enforce what it is empowered to demand.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Designers should ensure that the central government’s instruments (money, troops, courts) and institutional independence are adequate to carry its nominal competences into effect; otherwise nominal powers become ineffective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Division of labor between central and provincial authorities to fit population exigencies
rubrics_metrics.description: The law adapts itself to the exigencies of the population; population does not conform to the exigencies of the law. Congress regulates principal measures while details of administration are reserved to provincial legislatures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Federal systems should allocate general, rare, and overarching responsibilities to the center and daily, local, and specific matters to local governments so laws fit local customs and needs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Federalism combines advantages of small and large states
rubrics_metrics.description: The Federal system aims to unite the twofold advantages resulting from a small and from a large territory — e.g., freedom and public spirit of small states with strength and civilization of great nations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluations should consider whether the system actually preserves local vigor (township energy, provincial patriotism) while giving the Union sufficient international power and resources (commerce, navy, reach).

rubrics_metrics.name: Public/political sophistication among citizens is required
rubrics_metrics.description: The federal system is complex and demands the daily exercise of a considerable share of discretion on the part of those it governs; it presupposes a variety of information and excellence of discretion in the people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A federal constitution is ill-suited to peoples unaccustomed to self-government or lacking political knowledge; successful federalism requires civic competence down to local levels (ability to distinguish federal vs state obligations and jurisdictions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Two sovereignties create inevitable complexity and collisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Two sovereignties are necessarily in presence of each other; the legislator cannot prevent collisions at certain points between State and Union authorities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mitigation: simplify and equalize actions by accurately defining each sovereignty’s sphere of authority; nonetheless some conflicts are intrinsic and must be expected and managed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clear delimitation of spheres to reduce conflict
rubrics_metrics.description: The legislator may simplify and equalize the action of the two sovereignties by limiting each of them to a sphere of authority accurately defined.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical design principle: draw precise constitutional boundaries between federal and state competences to lower friction and litigation (but realize it cannot remove all collision points).

rubrics_metrics.name: Underlying common interests and inducements to union are necessary
rubrics_metrics.description: The Federal compact cannot be lasting unless there exists in the communities a certain number of inducements to union which render common dependence agreeable and the task of the Government light.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beyond constitutional design, cultural, economic, geographic, and interest-based ties (trade, defense, shared institutions) must exist to sustain a federation; absence of such ties risks breakdown.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relative weakness of the central government is an inherent federal danger
rubrics_metrics.description: A divided sovereignty must always be less powerful than an entire supremacy; the relative weakness of the Government of the Union is a fatal defect inherent in the federal system.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Designers should recognize and seek institutional remedies (e.g., federal institutions with direct powers) but acknowledge limits: federal authority may always face superior local affections and prejudices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Local attachments and state sovereignty often trump abstract national sovereignty
rubrics_metrics.description: The sovereignty of the Union is an abstract being connected with few external objects; the sovereignty of the States is hourly perceptible and interwoven with citizens' daily lives and attachments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect that citizens' primary loyalties and remedies may lie with their State; federal designs must build popular identification with the Union or risk organized resistance in cases of widespread grievance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suitability of federalism depends on historical/cultural readiness
rubrics_metrics.description: A federal constitution like the American one may be profitless in other hands if the people do not possess the spirit and sense which give it life (e.g., Mexico copied the letter but lacked the spirit and failed).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Transplanting constitutional forms without the supporting social/political culture is risky; assess historical experience with self-government before adopting a federal model.

rubrics_metrics.name: Size and population composition affect republican stability
rubrics_metrics.description: All the passions fatal to republican institutions spread with increasing territory, while the virtues that maintain them do not augment proportionally; great republics are exposed to greater perils than small ones.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluation should weigh how ambition, parties, inequality, and political passions scale with territory and population; federal arrangements are aimed at mitigating those scaling problems but are not a panacea.

rubrics_metrics.name: Federalism reduces uniformity problems of centralized law
rubrics_metrics.description: In great centralized nations the legislator imparts uniformity that may not suit the diversity of customs and districts; confederations reserve details to provincial legislatures so the law adapts to local exigencies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A key measure of federal design quality is its capacity to allow legal variation where appropriate while retaining necessary national uniformity in core matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for institutions that promote peace and discourage interstate war
rubrics_metrics.description: Since collisions between sovereignties cannot be wholly avoided, legislators must encourage institutions that promote the maintenance of peace; the Federal compact requires inducements to union and institutions that dissuade confederate States from warfare.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessment should include whether constitutional and political mechanisms reduce incentives for interstate conflict (economic interdependence, common defense structures, dispute resolution).

rubrics_metrics.name: Geographic, cultural, and social affinities matter for durability
rubrics_metrics.description: Natural causes of union must exist between confederate peoples besides the laws; e.g., Maine and Georgia, separated by a thousand miles, may be more naturally united than Normandy and Brittany when affinities are present.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate federations not just on legal form but on underlying affinities: language, legal traditions, economic ties, and shared outlooks that make union feasible.
